questions.q: The area of the sector of a circle of radius 12 cm is $60\pi$ cm². The central angle of this sector is:
questions.solution:
A sector is a slice of the whole circle, and the slice's share of the area equals the angle's share of $360°$:

$\text{area of sector} = \dfrac{\theta}{360°} \times \pi r^{2}$

$60\pi = \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi \times 144$

Divide both sides by $\pi$:

$60 = \dfrac{144\theta}{360}$

$\theta = \dfrac{60 \times 360}{144} = \mathbf{150°}$

Leaving $\pi$ as a symbol until it cancels saves all the arithmetic — the question gave the area as $60\pi$ precisely so that it would.

**Sanity check:** the whole circle has area $144\pi$, and $60\pi$ is a little under half of it. A little under $180°$ is $150°$ ✓

questions.q: The length of an arc of a circle with radius 12 cm is $10\pi$ cm. The angle subtended by the arc at the centre of the circle is:
questions.solution:
The arc is the same fraction of the circumference that the angle is of $360°$:

$\text{arc length} = \dfrac{\theta}{360°} \times 2\pi r$

$10\pi = \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi \times 12$

Cancel $\pi$:

$10 = \dfrac{24\theta}{360} = \dfrac{\theta}{15}$

$\theta = \mathbf{150°}$

Notice this is the same answer as the sector-area question with the same radius — and that is no coincidence. Arc length and sector area are both just "$\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of the whole thing", one applied to the circumference and one to the area.

Learn the single idea rather than two formulas: **a sector is a fraction of a circle, and the fraction is $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$.**

questions.q: If the area of a sector of a circle of radius 36 cm is $54\pi$ cm², then the length of the corresponding arc of the sector is:
questions.solution:
There is a shortcut that avoids finding the angle at all:

$\text{area of sector} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times r \times (\text{arc length})$

$54\pi = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 36 \times l$

$54\pi = 18l \Rightarrow l = \mathbf{3\pi}$ cm

**The long way, as a check.** From the area, $\dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi \times 36^{2} = 54\pi$, so $\dfrac{\theta}{360} = \dfrac{54}{1296} = \dfrac{1}{24}$. Then the arc is $\dfrac{1}{24} \times 2\pi \times 36 = 3\pi$ cm ✓

Why the shortcut works: a thin sector is very nearly a triangle with base $l$ (the arc) and height $r$, and area $\tfrac{1}{2} \times$ base $\times$ height. Remarkably, the formula is exact for a sector of any size.

questions.q: The area of a circle of radius 14 cm is: (Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution:
$A = \pi r^{2} = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 \times 14$

Cancel the 7 into one of the 14s first — always easier than multiplying then dividing:

$= 22 \times 2 \times 14 = \mathbf{616}$ cm²

Option (A), $88$ cm, is the **circumference** $2\pi r = 2 \times \tfrac{22}{7} \times 14$ — the classic mix-up.

A quick way to tell them apart: area is measured in **square** centimetres and involves $r^{2}$; circumference is a plain length and involves $r$ to the first power. If your answer's units do not match what was asked, you have used the wrong formula.

Radii of $7$, $14$, $21$ and $28$ appear constantly in this chapter because they cancel neatly with $\tfrac{22}{7}$.

questions.q: If the circumference of a circle is 176 cm, then its radius is: (Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution:
$C = 2\pi r$

$176 = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times r = \dfrac{44r}{7}$

$r = \dfrac{176 \times 7}{44} = 4 \times 7 = \mathbf{28}$ cm

**Check:** $2 \times \tfrac{22}{7} \times 28 = 2 \times 22 \times 4 = 176$ ✓

The division $\tfrac{176}{44} = 4$ is the whole calculation; everything else is bookkeeping. When $\pi = \tfrac{22}{7}$, look for the 22 and the 7 to cancel before reaching for a calculator.

questions.q: The area of a quadrant of a circle of radius 7 cm is: (Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution:
A **quadrant** is a quarter of the circle — a sector with a $90°$ angle.

Whole circle: $\pi r^{2} = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 = 154$ cm²

Quadrant: $\dfrac{154}{4} = \mathbf{38.5}$ cm²

Or in one step: $\dfrac{90}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 = \dfrac{1}{4} \times 154 = 38.5$ cm².

The words are worth collecting, since the papers use them without explanation:

- **semicircle** — half the circle, angle $180°$
- **quadrant** — a quarter, angle $90°$
- **sector** — any slice, angle $\theta$
- **segment** — the region between a chord and its arc (not a slice from the centre)

questions.topic: Area of each of many sectors
questions.q:
A circle is divided into 16 identical sectors. If the radius of the circle is 7 cm, find the area of each sector in cm². (Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)

Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
questions.solution:
**Whole circle first:**

$A = \pi r^{2} = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 7 = 154$ cm²

**Sixteen identical sectors** share that area equally:

$\text{each} = \dfrac{154}{16} = \dfrac{77}{8} = 9.625 \approx \mathbf{9.63}$ cm²

You never need the angle, though it is $\dfrac{360°}{16} = 22.5°$ if you want to check the long way:

$\dfrac{22.5}{360} \times 154 = \dfrac{1}{16} \times 154 = 9.625$ ✓

"Identical sectors" is doing the work here. Equal slices means equal areas, so the problem is just a division — the same as cutting a pizza.

questions.q: Find the perimeter of a quadrant of a circle of radius 7 cm, in centimetres. (Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution:
The perimeter of a quadrant is **not** just the curved part. Walking around it you travel along three edges: two straight radii and one arc.

**The arc** is a quarter of the circumference:

$\dfrac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \dfrac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 = \dfrac{44}{4} = 11$ cm

**The two radii:** $7 + 7 = 14$ cm

**Total perimeter:** $11 + 14 = \mathbf{25}$ cm

This is the most common mistake in the chapter — answering $11$ cm, the arc alone. Trace the boundary with your finger: you cannot get back to where you started without walking along both straight edges.

The same applies to a sector of any angle: perimeter $= \text{arc} + 2r$.

questions.q:
Find the area, in cm², of a sector of a circle of radius 6 cm whose central angle is $60°$. (Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)

Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
questions.solution:
$\text{area} = \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^{2}$

$= \dfrac{60}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 36$

$= \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{792}{7}$

$= \dfrac{132}{7} \approx \mathbf{18.86}$ cm²

Simplify $\dfrac{60}{360}$ to $\dfrac{1}{6}$ before multiplying — it turns an awkward calculation into a short one.

**Sanity check:** the whole circle is $\tfrac{22}{7} \times 36 \approx 113.1$ cm², and a $60°$ sector is one sixth of that, about $18.9$ ✓

questions.q:
A circular ring is formed between two concentric circles of radii 7 cm and 3.5 cm. Find the area of the ring in cm². (Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)

Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
questions.solution:
The ring (an **annulus**) is the big circle with the small one punched out of it:

$\text{area} = \pi R^{2} - \pi r^{2} = \pi(R^{2} - r^{2})$

$= \dfrac{22}{7}\big(7^{2} - 3.5^{2}\big) = \dfrac{22}{7}\big(49 - 12.25\big) = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 36.75$

$= \mathbf{115.5}$ cm²

Factoring out the $\pi$ before subtracting means one multiplication instead of two.

**Sanity check:** the big circle is $154$ cm² and the small one is $38.5$ cm² — a quarter of the big one, since halving the radius quarters the area. $154 - 38.5 = 115.5$ ✓

That last point is worth keeping: **halve the radius and the area drops to a quarter**, because area depends on $r^{2}$.

questions.q: A chord of a circle of radius 10 cm subtends a right angle at the centre. Find the area of the corresponding **minor segment**. (Use $\pi = 3.14$)
questions.solution:
A **segment** is what is left when you cut the triangle off a sector — the region between the chord and its arc.

$\text{area of segment} = \text{area of sector} - \text{area of triangle}$

**Area of the sector** ($\theta = 90°$, $r = 10$):

$\dfrac{90}{360} \times 3.14 \times 100 = \dfrac{1}{4} \times 314 = 78.5$ cm²

**Area of the triangle.** The two radii are perpendicular, so it is right-angled with both legs equal to the radius:

$\dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 10 = 50$ cm²

**Area of the minor segment:**

$78.5 - 50 = \mathbf{28.5}$ cm²

The picture is a slice of pizza with the crust-side piece torn off: the sector is the whole slice, the triangle is the pointed part, and the segment is the curved offcut.

When the angle is $90°$ the triangle is easy — half of $r^{2}$. At $60°$ the triangle is equilateral, area $\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}r^{2}$; those two cases cover almost every board question on segments.

questions.q: A horse is tied to a peg at one corner of a square grassy field of side 15 m by means of a 5 m long rope. Find the area of the field that the horse can graze. (Use $\pi = 3.14$)
questions.solution:
**Picture the region the horse can reach.** The rope sweeps out a circle of radius 5 m, but the two fences meeting at that corner are at right angles — so the horse can only cover the **quarter** of that circle lying inside the field.

$\text{grazed area} = \dfrac{90}{360} \times \pi r^{2} = \dfrac{1}{4} \times 3.14 \times 5^{2}$

$= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 3.14 \times 25 = \dfrac{78.5}{4} = \mathbf{19.625}$ m²

The side of the field, 15 m, is deliberately much longer than the rope. It is there to tell you the horse never reaches another corner — so the grazed region is a clean quarter-circle and nothing is cut off.

If the rope were longer than the side, parts of the quarter-circle would spill past the far corners and would have to be subtracted. Always check the rope against the field before assuming a tidy quadrant.

questions.topic: Areas swept by a clock hand
questions.q: The minute hand of a clock is 14 cm long. Find the area swept by the minute hand in 5 minutes. (Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution:
**Turn the time into an angle.** The minute hand goes all the way round — $360°$ — in 60 minutes, so in one minute it turns $6°$, and in 5 minutes:

$\theta = 5 \times 6° = 30°$

**Now it is an ordinary sector**, with $r = 14$ cm (the length of the hand):

$\text{area} = \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^{2} = \dfrac{30}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 \times 14$

$= \dfrac{1}{12} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 196$

$= \dfrac{1}{12} \times 616 = \dfrac{154}{3} \approx \mathbf{51.33}$ cm²

Two things to keep straight in clock questions. The **hand's length is the radius**, and the **time converts to an angle** at $6°$ per minute for the minute hand.

(The hour hand is slower: $360°$ in 12 hours, so $30°$ per hour or $0.5°$ per minute.)

questions.q: Find the perimeter and the area of a semicircular protractor of diameter 14 cm. (Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution:
Diameter 14 cm means radius $r = 7$ cm.

**Area.** A semicircle is half a circle:

$\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 = \dfrac{154}{2} = \mathbf{77}$ cm²

**Perimeter.** Walk around the edge: half the circumference, **then back along the straight diameter**.

curved part $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2\pi r = \pi r = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 = 22$ cm

straight part $= $ diameter $= 14$ cm

$\text{perimeter} = 22 + 14 = \mathbf{36}$ cm

The area really is half the circle's, but the perimeter is **not** half the circumference — cutting a circle in two creates a new straight edge that was not there before.

Same lesson as the quadrant: for area you take a fraction, for perimeter you trace the boundary.

questions.q: The circumferences of two circles are in the ratio $2 : 3$. Find the ratio of their areas.
questions.solution:
**Circumference is proportional to the radius**, since $C = 2\pi r$. So if the circumferences are in the ratio $2 : 3$, the radii are too:

$\dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

**Area is proportional to the radius squared**, since $A = \pi r^{2}$:

$\dfrac{A_1}{A_2} = \dfrac{\pi r_1^{2}}{\pi r_2^{2}} = \left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^{2} = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{2} = \mathbf{\dfrac{4}{9}}$

So the areas are in the ratio $4 : 9$.

**Check with real numbers:** take $r_1 = 2$ and $r_2 = 3$. Circumferences $4\pi$ and $6\pi$ — ratio $2:3$ ✓. Areas $4\pi$ and $9\pi$ — ratio $4:9$ ✓

The general rule, and it holds for every similar shape, not just circles: **lengths scale by $k$, areas scale by $k^{2}$.** It is the same fact behind similar triangles' areas being in the ratio of the squares of their sides.
